## What’s This Workshop?

- This workshop is an introduction to using R.
- No prior knowledge is assumed.
- The goal is to make your time in POS 5737 and future methods courses a little easier.
  - R is fairly complicated to use, but we’re going to get as far as we can this week!

## Introductions!

- Taylor
- Rexburg, Idaho
- American Behaviorist
- Research interest: voting behavior, democratic backsliding, public opinion, experimental methods, political psychology
- I am starting my thrid-year in the program. 
- I am married with a 2 year old daughter and a baby girl on the way in September. 

## Ground Rules for the Class

- Please ask questions--feel free to interrupt at any time. The material will build fast so please make sure you understand each step before we move to the next one. 
- Look into Stack Exchange--this is a great resource when you run into coding issues. 
- Use the Help function in RStudio--we will talk more about how to do this.

## Welcome to FSU!

**As I'm sure you are aware, you are joining one of the best political science departments in the country.**
- This is the best department in the state of Florida. 
- FSU pulls above its weigh in publications in top journals 

Images Here

## What Graduate School Is—and Is Not

- This is not undergrad 2.0--it is less structred, you have more freedom.
- This is a lot of work.
  - Expect to read about 300 pages a week, at least 1 problem set, and occasional papers as well. 
- It is very rewarding, and you will learn A LOT. 


## How to Be Successful

**1) Go to class**

- Participate when you do go to class.
- Do the readings! 
  - Come to class with thoughts and comments about the readings. 
- Besides methods classes, the 2.5 hours of class are controlled by the students talking. It can get really awkward if no one has read. 

**2) Go to department functions.**

- About three hours of your contract are allotted to professionalization events.
- The colloquiums, job talks, and guest speakers are part of your paycheck. 

**3) Fulfill your GA and RA responsibilities.**

- Faculty differ in what they ask, but they are usually good about respecting the allotted time.
- If there is a problem, talk to Carlisle. 
- I have never heard of anyone being over worked or taken advantage of in these roles. 

## The Most Important Way to Be Successful: DO NOT RELY ON AI

- It can be very easy and inciting to get AI to summaries the readings for you, write the code for your problem sets, or do your work for you. 
- It is extremely hard to be successful at FSU if you rely heavily on AI. 
- A significant part of this program requires students to orally defend their theory, methods, and arguments. Relying on AI will make this very difficult. 
- Relying on AI summaries of the text or AI generated code will leave you confused and left behind as the courses move quickly through material. 

## How to Use AI Appropriately for Coding

- Make sure that you learn how to do the coding yourself first and then you can use AI to help you problem solve. 
- AI coding is still far from perfect. 
- You must be able to check the work the AI model did for you to ensure that your code is correct. 
- Best approach
  1. Work through a problem on your own as best as you can. 
  2. If your code is returning errors, copy and paste the error into an AI model to help you problem solve. 
  3. If the AI generates code for you, pepper it with questions to ensure you fully understand what each line of code is doing. 

## Managing Graduate School

- Impostor syndrome is real. Do your best not to let it get to you.
- FSU has therapy resources--while not all students need this, it is a great resource.
- Work together with your cohort. 
  - Cohorts that work together stay together. 
  - Collaboration is welcomed in most methods classes—just turn in your own work.
- Keep a schedule and learn when you work best.
- **Do things other than graduate school.**
  - Tallahassee and FSU have plenty to explore- Wakulla Springs, 30A beaches, St. George Island, etc.

## Using R as a Calculator

```r
1 + 1
```

```text
[1] 2
```

```r
1 + 3
```

```text
[1] 4
```

```r
100000000000000 * 21000000000000
```

```text
[1] 2.1e+27
```

```r
sqrt(400)
```

```text
[1] 20
```

Take a moment and perform the following calculations:

- $9 + 10$
- $9 \times 10$

R defaults to the natural logarithm, $\ln$ or $\log_e$.

## Objects and Scalars

```r
b <- 2
b + 2
```


```r
# Use # to leave comments in your code.
## Assign 2 to the letter b.
b <- 2

## Add b and 2.
b + 2
```

Using `2 + 2` would be easier here; this example demonstrates how objects work.

## Functions


## Strings

```r
# Words are represented as character strings.
"Hello World"
```

```text
[1] "Hello World"
```

## Strings Cannot Be Used as Numbers

```r
"Hello World" + 2
```

```text
Error in "Hello World" + 2: non-numeric argument to binary operator
```

The same is true when the string contains a number.

```r
"3" + 2
```

```text
Error in "3" + 2: non-numeric argument to binary operator
```

## Converting Strings to Numbers

```r
as.numeric("3") + 2
```

```text
[1] 5
```

```r
library(tidyverse)
parse_number("3") + 2
```

```text
[1] 5
```

## `parse_number()` Extracts a Number

```r
parse_number("himothy316") + 2
```

```text
[1] 318
```

```r
as.numeric("himothy316") + 2
```

```text
[1] NA
```

This difference is useful when numbers are embedded in data labels.

```r
parse_number("ideo2")
```

```text
[1] 2
```

## Vectors

- Working with only one number is not realistic.
- Instead, we work with collections of values called **vectors**.

Common types include:

- **Numeric:** `1.1`, `2`, and `100`
- **Character:** `"Republican"`, `"Democratic"`, and `"Independent"`
- **Factor:** ordered categories
- **Logical:** `TRUE` or `FALSE`

## Numeric Vectors

```r
a <- c(5, 10, 15, 100)
a
```

```text
[1]   5  10  15 100
```

```r
a / 5
mean(a) # Congratulations: you're doing statistics.
```

```text
[1]  1  2  3 20
[1] 32.5
```

## Character Vectors

```r
p <- c("Republican", "Democrat", "Republican", "Independent")
p
```

```text
[1] "Republican" "Democrat" "Republican" "Independent"
```

Numeric functions do not work on character vectors.

```r
p * 3
```

```text
Error in p * 3: non-numeric argument to binary operator
```

## Escape Sequences in Strings

- `\n` starts a new line.
- `\t` inserts a tab.

```r
cat("Repu\nblican")
cat("Demo\tcrat")
```

```text
Repu
blican
Demo    crat
```

## Factor Vectors

```r
p1 <- c("Republican", "Republican", "Democrat", "Other")
class(p1)
table(p1)
```

```text
[1] "character"
p1
  Democrat      Other Republican
         1          1          2
```

Problem: the ordering is odd, and Independents are missing.

```r
pid <- factor(
  p1,
  levels = c("Republican", "Independent", "Democrat", "Other")
)
```

## Checking the Factor

```r
class(pid)
table(pid)
```

```text
[1] "factor"
pid
 Republican Independent    Democrat       Other
          2           0           1           1
```

## Missing Values

- Missing values are denoted by `NA`.
- Some functions preserve them.

```r
x <- c(1, 4, 7, NA, 2)
log(x)
```

```text
[1] 0.0000000 1.3862944 1.9459101 NA 0.6931472
```

```r
sum(x)
sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)
```

```text
[1] NA
[1] 14
```

## Logical Operators

Logical operators test whether conditions hold.

| Operator | Syntax |
|:--|:--:|
| Less than | `<` |
| Less than or equal to | `<=` |
| Exactly equal to | `==` |
| Greater than or equal to | `>=` |
| Greater than | `>` |
| Not equal to | `!=` |
| Or | `\|` |
| And | `&` |

## Data Frames and Tibbles

- Most data will be organized as **data frames** or **tibbles**.
- Think of a data frame or tibble as a collection of vectors.

```r
data.frame(
  name = c("John", "Jacob", "Jingleheimer Schmidt"),
  ideo = c(1, 4, 7),
  sex  = c("Male", "Male", "Male")
) -> his_name
```

## Creating a Tibble

Install the tidyverse once from the console:

```r
install.packages("tidyverse")
```

```r
library(tidyverse)

tibble(
  name = c("John", "Jacob", "Jingleheimer Schmidt"),
  ideo = c(1, 4, 7),
  sex  = c("Male", "Male", "Male")
) -> his_name
```

## Calling a Column

The `$` operator extracts one column as a vector.

```r
his_name$name
his_name$ideo / 2
```

```text
[1] "John" "Jacob" "Jingleheimer Schmidt"
[1] 0.5 2.0 3.5
```

## Combining Vectors into a Tibble

```r
name <- c("John", "Jacob", "Jingleheimer Schmidt")
ideo <- c(1, 4, 7)
sex  <- c("Male", "Male", "Male")

tibble(name, ideo, sex)
```

```text
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  name                  ideo sex
  <chr>                <dbl> <chr>
1 John                     1 Male
2 Jacob                    4 Male
3 Jingleheimer Schmidt     7 Male
```

## Making Data Usable with `mutate()`

```r
his_name %>%
  mutate(
    ideo_cat = c("Very Conservative", "Moderate", "Very Liberal")
  )
```

```text
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  name                  ideo sex   ideo_cat
1 John                     1 Male  Very Conservative
2 Jacob                    4 Male  Moderate
3 Jingleheimer Schmidt     7 Male  Very Liberal
```

The `%>%` operator is a **pipe**. Insert it with Ctrl—or Command—Shift-M.

## The Base R Equivalent

```r
his_name$ideo_cat <- c(
  "Very Conservative",
  "Moderate",
  "Very Liberal"
)

his_name
```

## `mutate()` and `case_when()`

Use `case_when()` to create a variable conditionally.

```r
his_name %>%
  mutate(
    ideo_cat = case_when(
      ideo == 1 ~ "Very Conservative",
      ideo == 4 ~ "Moderate",
      ideo == 7 ~ "Very Liberal"
    )
  ) -> his_name_2

his_name_2
```

## `filter()`

Use `filter()` to keep rows matching a condition.

```r
his_name_2 %>%
  filter(ideo_cat == "Very Liberal")
```

```text
# A tibble: 1 × 4
  name                  ideo sex   ideo_cat
1 Jingleheimer Schmidt     7 Male  Very Liberal
```

## Removing Rows with `filter()`

Use `!=` to keep rows that are **not** equal to a value.

```r
his_name_2 %>%
  filter(ideo_cat != "Very Liberal")
```

```text
# A tibble: 2 × 4
  name   ideo sex   ideo_cat
1 John      1 Male  Very Conservative
2 Jacob     4 Male  Moderate
```

## Variable Names

Research data often arrive with unclear variable names.

```r
tibble(
  X1 = c(123, 124, 125, 126),
  X2 = c(1, 2, 4, 7),
  X3 = c("abortion", "health care", "guns", "police")
) -> data
```

What does each variable represent?

## Renaming Variables

Ask two questions:

- Is the name informative?
- Is the name easy to work with?

```r
data %>%
  rename(
    id    = X1,
    ideo  = X2,
    issue = X3
  )
```

## Informative Names Can Still Be Awkward

```r
tibble(
  "ID Number" = c(123, 124, 125, 126),
  "Ideology Numeric" = c(1, 2, 4, 7),
  "Most Important Issue" = c(
    "abortion", "health care", "guns", "police"
  )
) -> data
```

The `clean_names()` function from **janitor** can fix them.

```r
install.packages("janitor")
```

## Cleaning Variable Names

Use `::` to call one function directly from a package.

```r
data %>%
  janitor::clean_names() -> data

data
```

```text
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  id_number ideology_numeric most_important_issue
1       123                1 abortion
2       124                2 health care
3       125                4 guns
4       126                7 police
```

## Selecting Variables

Use `select()` with either a variable name or position.

```r
data %>% select(most_important_issue)
data %>% select(3)
```

## Selecting Rows with `slice()`

Suppose the first row contains variable names rather than data.

```r
tibble(
  country = c("country", "USA", "China", "Germany"),
  wars    = c("wars", 2, 4, 5),
  pres    = c("pres", 1, 0, 1),
  par     = c("par", "Congress", "None", "Parliament")
) -> country

country
```

## Removing Rows and Columns

Use a minus sign to remove a row with `slice()` or a column with `select()`.

```r
country %>%
  slice(-1) -> country

country %>%
  select(-wars)
```

## More on Cleaning

One of the last cleaning steps is ensuring variables use the proper types.

```text
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  country wars  pres  par
  <chr>   <chr> <chr> <chr>
1 USA     2     1     Congress
2 China   4     0     None
3 Germany 5     1     Parliament
```

`wars` and `pres` are character variables but need to be numeric.

## Practice with Data Cleaning

```r
tibble(
  country = c("country", "USA", "China", "Germany"),
  wars    = c("wars", 2, 4, 5),
  pres    = c("pres", 1, 0, 1),
  par     = c("par", "Congress", "None", "Parliament")
) -> country
```

Use `slice()`, `parse_number()`, and `mutate()` to clean it.

## Data-Cleaning Solution

```r
country %>%
  slice(-1) %>%
  mutate(
    wars = parse_number(wars),
    pres = parse_number(pres)
  )
```

```text
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  country  wars  pres par
1 USA         2     1 Congress
2 China       4     0 None
3 Germany     5     1 Parliament
```

## Reading Data into R

Most data will come from a file, often a CSV.

```r
library(tidyverse)

# Base R
anes <- read.csv("anes.csv")

# tidyverse
anes <- read_csv("anes.csv")
```

Running these lines sequentially leaves only the second version of `anes` in the global environment.

## Working Directories

The previous code works only if the file is in your **working directory**.

```r
setwd("C:/Users/Austin/path/to/file")
anes <- read.csv("anes.csv")
```

On Windows, use forward slashes and place the path inside quotation marks.

## More on Working Directories

- Change the working directory with `setwd()`.
- Check it with `getwd()`.
- Alternatives:
  - Open R by opening an R script.
  - Specify the full path in your code.
  - Work inside an R project.

```r
library(tidyverse)
anes <- read_csv("C:/Users/Austin/path/to/file/anes.csv")
```

## Practice: Olympics Data

From the course website under Day 1, download the Olympics data and:

1. Read it with both `read_csv()` and `read.csv()`.
2. Keep only country, winter, and summer with `select()`.
3. Rename the variables clearly.
4. Create a total-medals variable.
5. Use `filter()` to show one country.
6. Use `filter()` to remove one country.

## `rowwise()` Code

```r
# Replace data with the name of your own data frame.
data %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate()
```

## Olympics Data: Complete Solution

```r
library(tidyverse)

# 1. Read the data.
read.csv("olympics.csv") -> olympics
read_csv("olympics.csv")

# 2. Keep only the variables we want.
olympics %>%
  select(X0, X1, X6) -> olympics

# 3. Rename the variables.
olympics %>%
  rename(
    country = X0,
    summer  = X1,
    winter  = X6
  ) -> olympics
```

## Olympics Data: Solution, Continued

```r
# 4. Create the total-medals variable.
olympics %>%
  slice(-1) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    total = sum(parse_number(summer), parse_number(winter))
  ) -> olympics

# 5. Keep only Germany.
olympics %>%
  filter(country == "Germany")

# 6. Remove Chile.
olympics %>%
  filter(country != "Chile")
```
